Where it began

W. G. Grace was born on 18 July 1848 at Downend, then a country village a few miles from Bristol. He grew up in a house that lived and breathed the game. An orchard was cleared to make a practice pitch, everyone at home was expected to join in, and even the dogs were sent out to field. He later claimed he first picked up a bat at the age of two.

His elder brother E. M. was a fine cricketer, and his younger brother Fred followed them both into the Gloucestershire and England sides. Gilbert, as the family knew him, first played for the local club at nine. By sixteen he had played at The Oval and at Lord's, and stood six feet two.

The player

His first-class career ran from 1865 to 1908, 44 seasons in all. In 1871 he became the first man to make 2,000 runs in a season, finishing with 2,739. In 1873 he was the first to take 100 wickets and score 1,000 runs in one summer, a feat he managed eight times. In August 1876 he hit 344 for MCC at Canterbury, the first triple hundred in first-class cricket, and within the week added 177 and 318 not out.

Test cricket only began when he was in his late twenties. On his debut in 1880 he made 154 at The Oval, England's first Test hundred, with E. M. and Fred in the same side: the first time three brothers had played together in a Test. He played 22 Tests, all against Australia, scoring 1,098 runs at 32.29 with two hundreds and a best of 170. He captained England 13 times and won eight.

What made him special

Grace is often called the father of modern batting. He usually opened, handled fast bowling with ease and seemed to own every stroke. He could bowl, too, taking 191 wickets in 1875 with a best of 10 for 49, and he was a fine outfielder who could throw a cricket ball 122 yards.

His Test figures look modest beside the rest, but Tests came late, and he was past thirty by his first. Books were never his strong suit either. He did not qualify as a doctor until he was 31, the cricket having a habit of getting in the way of his studies.

Away from the middle

Once qualified, in 1879, he ran a practice in Easton, a poorer part of Bristol, where his patients remembered him fondly. His black beard and red and yellow MCC cap made him instantly recognisable. He was called The Champion, then The Doctor, and in later years The Old Man. As a young man he won the 440 yards hurdles at the National Olympian Games in 1866 and played football for the Wanderers, and later in life he took up golf, lawn bowls and curling. Wisden named him one of its Cricketers of the Year.

And finally

In 1869 he made 122 out of 173 on a difficult pitch, and the cricketer Tom Emmett suggested he ought to be made to bat with a smaller bat. For almost forty years more, bowlers up and down the land would have seconded the motion.
